```{r simulation-setup, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}
library(tidyverse)
library(spatstat.geom)
library(spatstat.random)

set.seed(2409)

# Shared settings -------------------------------------------------------------
region_side <- 20
region_area <- region_side^2
plot_radius <- 1
tree_abundance <- 500
n_repeats <- 2000
blue <- rgb(0.16, 0.32, 0.75)
red <- rgb(0.82, 0.1, 0.26)

# Count trees that occur in at least one circular plot.
count_in_plots <- function(trees, centres, radius = plot_radius) {
  inside <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(centres)), function(j) {
    (trees$x - centres$x[j])^2 + (trees$y - centres$y[j])^2 <= radius^2
  }, logical(nrow(trees)))
  sum(rowSums(inside) > 0)
}

# Place circular plots at random, rejecting candidates that overlap an
# accepted plot. Plot centres stay at least one radius from the region edge.
random_nonoverlap_centres <- function(n, side = region_side,
                                      radius = plot_radius,
                                      x_bounds = c(0, side)) {
  centres <- tibble(x = numeric(), y = numeric())
  attempts <- 0
  while (nrow(centres) < n && attempts < 10000) {
    candidate <- tibble(x = runif(1, x_bounds[1] + radius, x_bounds[2] - radius),
                        y = runif(1, radius, side - radius))
    far_enough <- nrow(centres) == 0 ||
      all((centres$x - candidate$x)^2 + (centres$y - candidate$y)^2 >=
            (2 * radius)^2)
    if (far_enough) centres <- bind_rows(centres, candidate)
    attempts <- attempts + 1
  }
  stopifnot(nrow(centres) == n)
  centres
}

stratified_centres <- function() {
  bind_rows(
    random_nonoverlap_centres(4, x_bounds = c(0, region_side / 2)) |>
      mutate(stratum = "West"),
    random_nonoverlap_centres(5, x_bounds = c(region_side / 2, region_side)) |>
      mutate(stratum = "East")
  )
}

# Randomize the origin of an otherwise regular grid while keeping all plots
# inside the survey region. Illustrative maps use the centred grid itself.
random_start <- function(centres, x_shift = c(-2, 2), y_shift = c(-2, 2)) {
  centres |>
    mutate(x = x + runif(1, x_shift[1], x_shift[2]),
           y = y + runif(1, y_shift[1], y_shift[2]))
}

# Coordinates used to draw circular plots with ggplot2.
circle_data <- function(centres, design, radius = plot_radius) {
  theta <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)
  map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(centres)), function(j) {
    tibble(x = centres$x[j] + radius * cos(theta),
           y = centres$y[j] + radius * sin(theta),
           plot = paste(design, j), design = design)
  })
}

estimate_abundance <- function(trees, centres, radius = plot_radius) {
  if ("stratum" %in% names(centres)) {
    return(sum(vapply(split(centres, centres$stratum), function(plots) {
      coverage_h <- nrow(plots) * pi * radius^2 / (region_area / 2)
      count_in_plots(trees, plots, radius) / coverage_h
    }, numeric(1))))
  }
  coverage <- nrow(centres) * pi * radius^2 / region_area
  count_in_plots(trees, centres, radius) / coverage
}

theme_sampling <- theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90"),
        legend.position = "none")

# Example 1: increasing sampling coverage -------------------------------------
effort_centres <- list(
  `9 plots`  = expand_grid(x = seq(3, 17, length.out = 3),
                           y = seq(3, 17, length.out = 3)),
  `16 plots` = expand_grid(x = seq(2.5, 17.5, length.out = 4),
                           y = seq(2.5, 17.5, length.out = 4)),
  `25 plots` = expand_grid(x = seq(2, 18, length.out = 5),
                           y = seq(2, 18, length.out = 5))
)

uniform_example <- tibble(x = runif(tree_abundance, 0, region_side),
                          y = runif(tree_abundance, 0, region_side))

effort_map_points <- imap_dfr(effort_centres, function(centres, label) {
  uniform_example |>
    mutate(sampled = vapply(seq_len(n()), function(i) {
      any((x[i] - centres$x)^2 + (y[i] - centres$y)^2 <= plot_radius^2)
    }, logical(1)), design = label)
}) |>
  mutate(design = factor(design, levels = names(effort_centres)))
effort_map_circles <- imap_dfr(effort_centres, circle_data)
effort_map_circles <- effort_map_circles |>
  mutate(design = factor(design, levels = names(effort_centres)))

effort_map <- ggplot(effort_map_points, aes(x, y, colour = sampled)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.45) +
  geom_path(data = effort_map_circles,
            aes(x, y, group = plot), inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey75", `TRUE` = blue)) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, region_side), ylim = c(0, region_side), expand = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~design, nrow = 1) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_sampling

effort_results <- map_dfr(seq_len(n_repeats), function(rep) {
  imap_dfr(effort_centres, function(centres, label) {
    margin <- min(min(centres$x) - plot_radius,
                  region_side - plot_radius - max(centres$x))
    tibble(replicate = rep, design = label,
           estimate = estimate_abundance(
             uniform_example,
             random_start(centres, c(-margin, margin), c(-margin, margin))))
  })
}) |>
  mutate(design = factor(design, levels = names(effort_centres)))

effort_summary <- effort_results |>
  group_by(design) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(estimate), variance = var(estimate), .groups = "drop")

effort_hist <- ggplot(effort_results, aes(estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 20, boundary = 0, fill = blue,
                 colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = tree_abundance, colour = red, linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~design, nrow = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(200, 800)) +
  labs(x = expression(hat(N)), y = "Number of surveys") + theme_sampling

ggsave("figures/juniper/coverage-designs-fixedpop.pdf", effort_map, width = 9, height = 3)
ggsave("figures/juniper/coverage-histograms-fixedpop.pdf", effort_hist, width = 9, height = 3)

# Example 2: sampling a west-to-east density gradient -------------------------
systematic_centres <- expand_grid(x = c(3, 10, 17), y = c(3, 10, 17))
preferential_centres <- expand_grid(x = c(11, 14.5, 18), y = c(3, 10, 17))

# f(x) is proportional to x^2, so inverse-transform sampling gives x = L U^(1/3).
gradient_population <- function(n = tree_abundance) {
  tibble(x = region_side * runif(n)^(1/3),
         y = runif(n, 0, region_side))
}

gradient_example <- gradient_population()
gradient_example_centres <- list(
  Systematic = systematic_centres,
  Random = random_nonoverlap_centres(9),
  Stratified = stratified_centres(),
  `Eastern-biased` = preferential_centres
)

gradient_map_points <- imap_dfr(gradient_example_centres,
                                ~mutate(gradient_example, design = .y)) |>
  mutate(design = factor(design,
                         levels = c("Systematic", "Random", "Stratified", "Eastern-biased")))
gradient_map_circles <- imap_dfr(gradient_example_centres, circle_data)
gradient_map_circles <- gradient_map_circles |>
  mutate(design = factor(design,
                         levels = c("Systematic", "Random", "Stratified", "Eastern-biased")))
gradient_map <- ggplot(gradient_map_points, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_vline(data = tibble(design = factor("Stratified",
               levels = levels(gradient_map_points$design))),
             xintercept = region_side / 2, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(colour = blue, size = 0.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_path(data = gradient_map_circles,
            aes(x, y, group = plot), inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.35) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, region_side), ylim = c(0, region_side), expand = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~design, nrow = 1) + labs(x = "West  →  East", y = NULL) + theme_sampling

gradient_results <- map_dfr(seq_len(n_repeats), function(rep) {
  layouts <- list(Systematic = random_start(systematic_centres),
                  Random = random_nonoverlap_centres(9),
                  Stratified = stratified_centres(),
                  `Eastern-biased` = random_start(
                    preferential_centres, c(-1, 1), c(-2, 2)))
  imap_dfr(layouts, function(centres, label) {
    tibble(replicate = rep, design = label,
           estimate = estimate_abundance(gradient_example, centres))
  })
}) |>
  mutate(design = factor(design,
                         levels = c("Systematic", "Random", "Stratified", "Eastern-biased")))

gradient_summary <- gradient_results |>
  group_by(design) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(estimate), variance = var(estimate), .groups = "drop")

gradient_hist <- ggplot(gradient_results, aes(estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 25, boundary = 0, fill = blue,
                 colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = tree_abundance, colour = red, linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~design, nrow = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1200)) +
  labs(x = expression(hat(N)), y = "Number of surveys") + theme_sampling

ggsave("figures/juniper/gradient-designs-fixedpop.pdf", gradient_map, width = 9, height = 3)
ggsave("figures/juniper/gradient-histograms-fixedpop.pdf", gradient_hist, width = 9, height = 3)

# Example 3: sampling a clustered population ----------------------------------
survey_window <- owin(c(0, region_side), c(0, region_side))

# rThomas generates parent points and Gaussian clusters around them. We retain
# 500 offspring so every realization has the same true abundance.
clustered_population <- function(n = tree_abundance) {
  repeat {
    pattern <- rThomas(kappa = 0.08, scale = 0.7, mu = 17,
                       win = survey_window)
    if (pattern$n >= n) {
      keep <- sample.int(pattern$n, n)
      return(tibble(x = pattern$x[keep], y = pattern$y[keep]))
    }
  }
}

cluster_example <- clustered_population()
cluster_example_centres <- list(
  Systematic = systematic_centres,
  Random = random_nonoverlap_centres(9),
  Stratified = stratified_centres(),
  `Eastern-biased` = preferential_centres
)
cluster_map_points <- imap_dfr(cluster_example_centres,
                               ~mutate(cluster_example, design = .y)) |>
  mutate(design = factor(design,
                         levels = c("Systematic", "Random", "Stratified", "Eastern-biased")))
cluster_map_circles <- imap_dfr(cluster_example_centres, circle_data)
cluster_map_circles <- cluster_map_circles |>
  mutate(design = factor(design,
                         levels = c("Systematic", "Random", "Stratified", "Eastern-biased")))
cluster_map <- ggplot(cluster_map_points, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_vline(data = tibble(design = factor("Stratified",
               levels = levels(cluster_map_points$design))),
             xintercept = region_side / 2, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey45", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(colour = blue, size = 0.5, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_path(data = cluster_map_circles,
            aes(x, y, group = plot), inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.35) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, region_side), ylim = c(0, region_side), expand = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~design, nrow = 1) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_sampling

cluster_results <- map_dfr(seq_len(n_repeats), function(rep) {
  layouts <- list(Systematic = random_start(systematic_centres),
                  Random = random_nonoverlap_centres(9),
                  Stratified = stratified_centres(),
                  `Eastern-biased` = random_start(
                    preferential_centres, c(-1, 1), c(-2, 2)))
  imap_dfr(layouts, function(centres, label) {
    tibble(replicate = rep, design = label,
           estimate = estimate_abundance(cluster_example, centres))
  })
}) |>
  mutate(design = factor(design,
                         levels = c("Systematic", "Random", "Stratified", "Eastern-biased")))

cluster_summary <- cluster_results |>
  group_by(design) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(estimate), variance = var(estimate), .groups = "drop")

cluster_hist <- ggplot(cluster_results, aes(estimate)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, boundary = 0, fill = blue,
                 colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = tree_abundance, colour = red, linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~design, nrow = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1600)) +
  labs(x = expression(hat(N)), y = "Number of surveys") + theme_sampling

ggsave("figures/juniper/cluster-designs-fixedpop.pdf", cluster_map, width = 9, height = 3)
ggsave("figures/juniper/cluster-histograms-fixedpop.pdf", cluster_hist, width = 9, height = 3)
```

## Learning outcomes

By the end of the lecture and practical, you should be able to:

- Define a target population, survey region and suitable plot size.
- Compare simple random, stratified random and systematic sampling designs.
- Understand why complete detection is important for plot sampling.
- Explain how sampling effort and spatial patterns affect bias and precision.
- Understand the binomial model for animal counts$^*$.
- Estimate abundance from plot counts, by hand and using R.
- Understand how uncertainty in abundance estimates is communicated and calculated in R.

## Why do we care how many there are?

- abundance is the number of individuals in a population ($N$)
- abundance is a key indicator of population status
- however, in most cases it's \alert{impossible to count all animals}
- lots of focus on estimating abundance in ecology
- why do you think this is?

# Plot sampling - basic ideas

## How do we estimate how many there are?

- define a survey region
    - area that contains all members of an focal population
    - closed to immigration and emigration

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, error=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results='hide'}

# function copied from "oSCR" package, which is not on CRAN. 
# copying here for ease of running. 
e2dist <- function(x, y){
  if (!is.matrix(x)) x <- as.matrix(x)
  if (!is.matrix(y)) y <- as.matrix(y)
  i <- sort(rep(1:nrow(y), nrow(x)))
  dvec <- sqrt((x[, 1] - y[i, 1])^2 + (x[, 2] - y[i, 2])^2)
  matrix(dvec, nrow = nrow(x), ncol = nrow(y), byrow = F)
}
  

pdf(file="figures/region.pdf",width = 4, height = 4)
par(oma=c(0,0,0,0),mar=c(1,1,1,1))

plots <- expand.grid(seq(2,8,length=3),seq(2,8,length=3))

points(pts,pch=16, cex=1.3, col=clr)
for(i in 1:nrow(plots)) draw.circle(x = plots[i,1],y = plots[i,2], radius = 0.75)

pdf(file="figures/region-with-plots-with-samplesize.pdf",width = 4, height = 4)

points(pts,pch=16, cex=1.3, col=clr)

samplesizeS <- c(sum(apply(e2dist(pts,strips[1:1000,])<0.5,1,sum)>0),
                 sum(apply(e2dist(pts,strips[1001:2000,])<0.5,1,sum)>0),
                 sum(apply(e2dist(pts,strips[2001:3000,])<0.5,1,sum)>0))
points(pts,pch=16, cex=1.3, col=clr)
abline(v=c(unique(strips[,1])-0.5,unique(strips[,1])+0.5),lty=2)
text(x = c(unique(strips[,1])),y=rep(0.1,3),labels = paste(samplesizeS), cex=1.6)
box(bty="o")
dev.off()
```

## How do we estimate how many there are?

- define a survey region
    - area that contains all members of an focal population
    - closed to immigration and emigration
- simplest solution would be to perform a census
    - count all the animals in the population
    - not possible for many (most?) populations in the wild

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=3.5cm, yshift=-2.5cm] at (current page){
\includegraphics[height=1.7in]{figures/region-with-points}};
\end{tikzpicture}


## How do we estimate how many there are?

- define a survey region
    - area that contains all members of an focal population
    - closed to immigration and emigration
- simplest solution would be to perform a census
    - count all the animals in the population
    - not possible for many (most?) populations in the wild
- plot sampling is one simple solution
    - sample a subset of the region
    - extrapolate / scale up

\node[xshift=-1cm, yshift=-2.7cm] at (current page){this lecture};
\node[xshift=1cm, yshift=-2.5cm] at (current page){$\rightarrow$};
\end{tikzpicture}


## Plot sampling

- sampling plots can be
    - circular 
    - strips (rectangular)
    - $\ldots$ or any shape actually

## Plot sampling

- sampling plots can be
    - circular 
    - strips (rectangular)
- plots placed within the survey region 
    - at random
    - systematically with a random starting point
    - this defines the **coverage**

## Plot sampling

- sampling plots can be
    - circular 
    - strips (rectangular)
- plots placed within the survey region 
    - at random
    - systematically with a random starting point
    - this defines the **coverage**
- generate data from plot sampling
    - count the number of animals inside each plot
    - this is the **sample** $(n)$

## Plot sampling

- sampling plots can be
    - circular 
    - strips (rectangular)
- plots placed within the survey region 
    - at random
    - systematically with a random starting point
    - this defines the **coverage**
- generate data from plot sampling
    - count the number of animals inside each plot
    - this is the **sample** $(n)$
- objective: \alert{estimate how many in the region}
    - we need to use statistics (an **estimator**)
    - we need to estimate **abundance** $(\hat{N})$

## Plot sampling - an intuitive estimator

An \alert{estimator} is a function that takes in data and outputs an estimate of the quantity of interest

## Plot sampling - an intuitive estimator

An \alert{estimator} is a function that takes in data and outputs an estimate of the quantity of interest

- the quantity of interest is abundance $(N)$
- the inputs for the plot sampling example are
    - the number of things seen $(n)$
    - the area covered by the plots $(a)$
    - the total area of the region of interest $(A)$
    - from this we calculate the *proportion* of the region surveyed $\big(p_c=\frac{a}{A}\big)$

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=-2.7cm] at (current page){
\includegraphics[height=1.5in]{figures/region-with-plots}};
\end{tikzpicture}


## Plot sampling - an intuitive estimator

An \alert{estimator} is a function that takes in data and outputs an estimate of the quantity of interest

- the quantity of interest is abundance $(N)$
- the inputs for the plot sampling example are
    - the number of things seen $(n)$
    - the area covered by the plots $(a)$
    - the total area of the region of interest $(A)$
    - also the *proportion* of the region surveyed $\big(p_c=\frac{a}{A}\big)$


Assuming plot densities are **representative of density in the whole region**, an estimate of abundance can be generated as a function of the data:

$$\hat{N} = \frac{n}{a}A$$

## Plot sampling - an intuitive estimator

An \alert{estimator} is a function that takes in data and outputs an estimate of the quantity of interest

- the quantity of interest is abundance $(N)$
- the inputs for the plot sampling example are
    - the number of things seen $(n)$
    - the area covered by the plots $(a)$
    - the total area of the region of interest $(A)$
    - also the *proportion* of the region surveyed $\big(p_c=\frac{a}{A}\big)$


Assuming plot densities are **representative of density in the whole region**, an estimate of abundance can be generated as a function of the data:

$$\hat{N}(n) = {\frac{n}{a}A =} \frac{n}{\frac{a}{A}}$$

## Plot sampling - an intuitive estimator

An \alert{estimator} is a function that takes in data and outputs an estimate of the quantity of interest

- the quantity of interest is abundance $(N)$
- the inputs for the plot sampling example are
    - the number of things seen $(n)$
    - the area covered by the plots $(a)$
    - the total area of the region of interest $(A)$
    - also the *proportion* of the region surveyed $\big(p_c=\frac{a}{A}\big)$


Assuming plot densities are **representative of density in the whole region**, an estimate of abundance can be generated as a function of the data:

$$\hat{N}(n) = {\frac{n}{a}A =} {\frac{n}{\frac{a}{A}}} = \frac{n}{p_c}$$

# Example 1: How many juniper trees?

## How many juniper trees?

**Ecological problem**: Juniper woodland is an important mountain ecosystem in Kyrgyzstan. Managers need effective monitoring strategies to estimate the number of trees and detect changes in abundance.

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=-3.35cm, yshift=-1.25cm] at (current page){
\includegraphics[height=1.25in]{figures/juniper/juniper1_rahmonov.png}};
\node[xshift=-0cm, yshift=-1.25cm] at (current page){
\includegraphics[height=1.25in]{figures/juniper/juniper3_rahmonov.png}};
\node[xshift=3.35cm, yshift=-1.25cm] at (current page){
\includegraphics[height=1.25in]{figures/juniper/juniper2_rahmonov.png}};
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=-3.85cm] at (current page){
\scriptsize All images by O. Rahmonov (Rahmonov et al., Environ Earth Sci (2017) 76:324)};
\end{tikzpicture}

## How many juniper trees?

**Ecological problem**: Juniper woodland is an important mountain ecosystem in Kyrgyzstan. Managers need effective monitoring strategies to estimate the number of trees and detect changes in abundance.

\vspace{0.5cm}

**Sampling problem**: How can you count *all* the juniper trees when they are spread across a large, mountainous area, and survey teams have limited time and resources?

## How many juniper trees?

**Ecological problem**: Juniper woodland is an important mountain ecosystem in Kyrgyzstan. Managers need effective monitoring strategies to estimate the number of trees and detect changes in abundance.

\vspace{0.35cm}

**Sampling problem**: How can you count *all* the juniper trees when they are spread across a large, mountainous area, and survey teams have limited time and resources?

\vspace{0.35cm}

**Sampling solution**: Sample a representative portion of the area and use the observed density to estimate abundance $\rightarrow$ plot sampling!

## Two ways to sample juniper trees

The survey region is 10 km by 10 km, so its total area is

$$A = 100\ \text{km}^2.$$

We compare two sampling designs:

- nine **circular plots**, each with radius 0.75 km
- three **strip transects**, each 1 km wide and 10 km long

We count every juniper tree inside each sampled plot.

## Sampling with circular plots

Summary of the sampling:

- number of plots: $9$
- radius of each plot: $r = 0.75$ km
- juniper trees observed: $n = 20$

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=3.15cm, yshift=-1.75cm] at (current page){
\includegraphics[height=2.35in]{figures/region-with-plots-with-samplesize}};
\end{tikzpicture}


## Calculating the area covered by one circular plot

- Input data:
  - Number of plots: $n = 9$
  - Radius of each plot: $r = 0.75$ km
  - Value of $\pi = 3.1416$

\vspace{0.25cm}

- The area of a circle is $S = \pi r^2$

\vspace{0.25cm}

- Squaring the radius: $r^2 = (0.75)^2= 0,75\times 0.75= 0.5625$

\vspace{0.25cm}

- Substituting into the area formula:
$$
S = 3.1416 \times 0.5625 = 1.76715 \text{ km}^2
$$

- This is the area of one circular plot.

## Sampling with circular plots

The total area covered by the nine circular plots is

$$a = 9\pi r^2 = 9\pi(0.75)^2 \approx 15.90\ \text{km}^2.$$

The proportion of the region covered is

$$p_c = \frac{a}{A} = \frac{15.90}{100} \approx 0.159.$$

Assuming tree density in the plots is representative of the region:

$$\hat{N} = \frac{n}{p_c} = \frac{20}{0.159} \approx \alert{126\ \text{juniper trees}}.$$

## Sampling with strip transects

Summary of the sampling:

- number of strips: $3$
- dimensions of each strip: 1 km by 10 km
- juniper trees observed: $n = 17 + 16 + 10 = 43$

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=3.15cm, yshift=-1.75cm] at (current page){
\includegraphics[height=2.35in]{figures/region-with-strips-with-samplesize}};
\end{tikzpicture}

## Sampling with strip transects

The total area covered by the three strips is

$$a = 3(1 \times 10) = 30\ \text{km}^2.$$

The proportion of the region covered is

$$p_c = \frac{a}{A} = \frac{30}{100} = 0.30.$$

Assuming tree density in the strips is representative of the region:

$$\hat{N} = \frac{n}{p_c} = \frac{43}{0.30} \approx \alert{143\ \text{juniper trees}}.$$

## How many juniper trees?

The simulated survey region contains **125 juniper trees**.

\vspace{0.4cm}

| Sampling method | Area sampled | Trees counted | Estimated abundance |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Circular plots | 15.90 km$^2$ | 20 | $\hat{N} \approx 126$ |
| Strip transects | 30.00 km$^2$ | 43 | $\hat{N} \approx 143$ |

\vspace{0.4cm}

- the two samples give different estimates, even though they survey the same population
- a representative sample can give an estimate close to the true abundance
- larger coverage does not guarantee the closest estimate in one survey

## What assumptions did we make?

For either estimate to be reliable:

1. plots or strips are placed so that sampled density is representative of the whole region
2. every juniper tree inside a sampled area is detected and counted once
3. sampled areas do not overlap
4. the area of each plot and the total survey region are known

\vspace{0.4cm}

- \alert{but is this estimator any good}?

\vspace{0.4cm}

If trees are strongly clustered, or sampling avoids steep and inaccessible ground, what could happen to $\hat{N}$?

# What makes an estimator "good"?

## Is the estimator any good?

Estimators are judged on performance **on average**. Imagine we could repeat a survey again & again record the estimate each time.

## Is the estimator any good?

Estimators are judged on performance **on average**. Imagine we could repeat a survey again & again record the estimate each time.

- repeating 100000 times would generate the histogram
- repeating an infinite number times would generate the line
- this is the \alert{sampling distribution}
- describes what we expect if we did the survey again.

```{r, echo=FALSE, results='hide', message=FALSE, error=FALSE}
set.seed(2510)
nsamp <- rbinom(100000, 125, 0.159)
Nhat <- nsamp/0.159
Ndens <- density(Nhat,bw=8)

pdf(file="figures/sampdist-hist.pdf",width = 5.5, height = 4)
par(oma=c(0,0,0,0),mar=c(4,6,1,1))
hist(Nhat, probability = TRUE, col=adjustcolor(grn,0.2), breaks = seq(-0.5,125.5,1)/0.159,
     xlim=c(25,250), main="", las=1, ylab="",ylim=c(0,0.025), 
     xlab="Estimated abundance")
mtext(text = "Probability density", side = 2,line = 4.5)
lines(Ndens,lwd=3, col=bl)
box(bty="o")
dev.off()

# Illustrate bias by adding 25 trees to the same survey estimator.
Ndens <- density(Nhat + 25,bw=8)
sampling_mean <- mean(Nhat) + 25

pdf(file="figures/sampdist-dens-annotated.pdf",width = 5.5, height = 4)
par(oma=c(0,0,0,0),mar=c(4,6,1,1))
plot(Ndens,lwd=3, col=bl,xlim=c(25,250), main="", las=1, ylab="", 
     xlab="Estimated abundance", ylim=c(0,0.018))
polygon(x = c(Ndens$x,rev(Ndens$x)), y = c(Ndens$y,rep(0,length(Ndens$y))),
        border = bl,col = adjustcolor(col = bl,alpha.f = 0.1))
mtext(text = "Probability density", side = 2,line = 4.5)
arrows(x0 = sampling_mean,y0 = 0,
       x1 = sampling_mean,y1 = approx(Ndens$x, Ndens$y, sampling_mean)$y,
       length = 0, lwd=2)
arrows(x0 = 125,y0 = 0,
       x1 = 125,y1 = Ndens$y[which.min(abs(125-Ndens$x))],
       length = 0, lwd=2, lty=2)
arrows(x0 = sampling_mean, y0 = 0.008, x1 = 125, y1 = 0.008,
       code = 3, length = 0.1, lwd=2, col=rd)
arrows(x0 = 65, y0 = 0.002,
       x1 = 235, y1 = 0.002,
       code = 3, length = 0.1, lwd=2, col=rd)
text(x = 105, y = 0.008, labels = "Bias", cex=1.2, col=rd)
text(x = 95, y = 0.003, labels = "Variance", cex=1.2, col=rd)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lty=c(1,2), lwd=2, legend = c("Mean of sampling distribution", "Truth"),cex = 1)
box(bty="o")
dev.off()
```

\end{tikzpicture}

## Is the estimator any good?

Estimators are judged on performance **on average**. Imagine we could repeat a survey again & again record the estimate each time.

- *we can't do this of course, but helps conceptually*
- we will see how to get the sampling distribution in the next lecture
- for now lets assume we can repeat many times
- for now lets assume we also know the true abundance, $N$

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=-2.2cm] at (current page){
\includegraphics[height=1.75in]{figures/sampdist-hist}};
\end{tikzpicture}

## Is the estimator any good?

Properties of an estimator are derived from the sampling distribution

- suppose we know the sampling distribution and the true value $(N)$
- two properties of interest are:
    - bias
    - variance

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=-2.2cm] at (current page){
\includegraphics[height=1.75in]{figures/sampdist-dens-annotated}};
\end{tikzpicture}


## Estimator properties - Bias

- how close do the estimates get to the truth on average?
    - we call this the \alert{bias}
    - we want this to be 0 (ie, unbiased)  

\vspace{-0.2cm}
$$\text{Bias}\big(\hat{N}\big)=\mathbb{E}\big(\hat{N}\big) - N$$

```{r, echo=FALSE, results='hide', message=FALSE, error=FALSE}
set.seed(2510)
xy_bias_lowvar <- cbind(rnorm(15,-1.5,0.25),
                        rnorm(15,-1.5,0.25))
xy_nobias_lowvar <- cbind(rnorm(15,0,0.25),
                          rnorm(15,0,0.25))
xy_bias_hivar <- cbind(rnorm(15,-1.5,0.75),
                       rnorm(15,-1.5,0.75))
xy_nobias_hivar <- cbind(rnorm(15,0,0.75),
                         rnorm(15,0,0.75))


pdf(file="figures/target-bias.pdf",width = 8, height = 4)
par(mfrow=c(1,2),oma=c(0,0,0,0),mar=c(1,1,3,1))
plot(0,0,xlim=c(-4,4),ylim=c(-4,4), main = "Low bias",
     bty="n", xlab="",ylab="", type="n",
     xaxt="n",yaxt="n")
draw.circle(x = 0,y = 0,radius = 3.5)
draw.circle(x = 0,y = 0,radius = 2.5, col = adjustcolor(grn,0.2))
draw.circle(x = 0,y = 0,radius = 1.5, col="white")
draw.circle(x = 0,y = 0,radius = 0.5, col = adjustcolor(grn,0.2))
points(xy_nobias_lowvar, col=rd, cex=1.2, pch=16)

draw.circle(x = 0,y = 0,radius = 0.5, col = adjustcolor(grn,0.2))
```

## Estimator properties - Variance and precision

- how variable are the estimates from one survey to the next?
    - we call this the \alert{variance}
    - want low variance

\vspace{-0.2cm} 
$$\text{Var}\big(\hat{N}\big)$$
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=-2cm] at (current page){
\fbox{\includegraphics[height=1.6in]{figures/target-var}}};
\end{tikzpicture}

## Estimator properties - Variance and precision

- how variable are the estimates from one survey to the next?
    - alternatively the \alert{precision}
    - want high precision

\vspace{-0.2cm}
$$\text{Precision}\big(\hat{N}\big)=\frac{1}{\text{Var}\big(\hat{N}\big)}$$
\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=-2cm] at (current page){
\fbox{\includegraphics[height=1.6in]{figures/target-prec}}};
\end{tikzpicture}

## Estimator properties

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=-0.8cm] at (current page){
\fbox{\includegraphics[height=2.5in]{figures/target-quad}}};
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=3.0cm] at (current page){\Large{\textbf{Bias}}};
\node[xshift=-4.4cm, yshift=-0.8cm] at (current page){\Large{\textbf{Precision}}};
\end{tikzpicture}

## Estimator properties

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=-0.8cm] at (current page){
\fbox{\includegraphics[height=2.5in]{figures/dens-quad}}};
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=3.0cm] at (current page){\Large{\textbf{Bias}}};
\node[xshift=-4.4cm, yshift=-0.8cm] at (current page){\Large{\textbf{Precision}}};
\end{tikzpicture}

## Estimator properties

Ideally, estimator has no bias and the smallest variance possible

- Low bias is good:
    - estimates equal to the true value on average
    - if variance is high, any single estimate may still be far from truth

- Low variance / high precision is good 
    - estimates close to what it would be on average
    - if bias is high, a single estimate will likely be far from truth

- Often a trade-off between estimator bias and variance
    - low bias achieved by providing estimates with greater spread (more variance)
    - lower variance constrain estimates too much and cause greater bias
    - must look for a compromise between these two key properties
    
## Estimator properties - consistency

Estimator consistency is a desirable property: sampling distribution steadily \alert{shrinks towards the true value} as more data are collected.

- concerns bias & precision
- as sample size increases
    - variance decreases
    - sampling distribution shrinks toward the truth
    - any single estimate will have smaller bias (although average bias of the distribution does not change)
- estimate will be
    - *imprecise* if only bias shrinks
    - *inaccurate* if only variance shrinks


# Example 3: Sampling coverage

## Does increasing coverage improve the estimate?

**Sampling question**: What happens to estimator variance when we increase the number of circular plots?

\vspace{0.4cm}

We use a larger survey region containing **500 uniformly distributed juniper trees**:

- region: 20 km by 20 km, so $A = 400$ km$^2$
- plot radius: $r = 1$ km
- sampling effort: 9, 16, or 25 non-overlapping plots
- the same population is sampled by all three designs in each replicate

## Increasing the number of plots

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.98\textwidth]{figures/juniper/coverage-designs-fixedpop.pdf}
\end{center}

Grey trees are outside the plots; blue trees are sampled.

## Increasing the number of plots

The area sampled and proportional coverage increase with effort:

| Number of plots | Area sampled, $a$ | Coverage, $p_c=a/A$ |
|--:|--:|--:|
| 9  | $9\pi(1)^2=28.27$ km$^2$ | 0.071 |
| 16 | $16\pi(1)^2=50.27$ km$^2$ | 0.126 |
| 25 | $25\pi(1)^2=78.54$ km$^2$ | 0.196 |

For every survey we estimate abundance using

$$\hat N=\frac{n}{p_c}.$$

## Increasing coverage reduces estimator variance

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.98\textwidth]{figures/juniper/coverage-histograms-fixedpop.pdf}
\end{center}

The population is held fixed while the systematic grid origin varies. The red line is the true abundance, $N=500$.

## Increasing coverage reduces estimator variance

Results from 2,000 repeated surveys:

```{r coverage-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(effort_summary, digits = c(NA, 1, 0),
             col.names = c("Sampling effort", "Mean estimate", "Variance"))
```

\vspace{0.3cm}

- all three estimators are centred close to the true abundance
- with more plots, more trees are counted in each survey
- the sampling distribution becomes narrower: **increasing coverage reduces variance**

# Example 4: Spatial variation in density

## When density varies across the region

Juniper density may vary with elevation, slope, soils, or human disturbance.

Here density increases from west to east:

$$\lambda(x) \propto x^2.$$

The fixed population contains **500 trees**, but many more occur in the eastern part of the region.

## Four sampling designs

We compare nine non-overlapping circular plots placed:

1. **systematically** across the whole region in a 3x3 grid
2. **at random**, with a new arrangement for every survey
3. **stratified random**: four in the west, five in the east
4. **preferentially**, using a 3x3 grid in the high-density east

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.98\textwidth]{figures/juniper/gradient-designs-fixedpop.pdf}
\end{center}

All designs use the same effort and the same estimator, $\hat N=n/p_c$. Stratified sampling calculates $\hat N=n/p_c$ in each stratum and sums these.

## Systematic sampling represents the region

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.98\textwidth]{figures/juniper/gradient-histograms-fixedpop.pdf}
\end{center}

The population is held fixed while survey locations vary. The red line is the true abundance, $N=500$.

## Systematic sampling represents the region

Results from 2,000 repeated surveys:

```{r gradient-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(gradient_summary, digits = c(NA, 1, 0),
             col.names = c("Sampling design", "Mean estimate", "Variance"))
```

\vspace{0.3cm}

- systematic plots spread effort across the full density gradient
- random plots can concentrate in low- or high-density areas
- stratification samples both halves; weight their counts separately
- eastern-biased plots consistently sample high density and overestimate abundance

# Example 5: Clustered trees

## When juniper trees are clustered

Junipers may occur in patches because suitable microsites are patchy and dispersal is local.

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.98\textwidth]{figures/juniper/cluster-designs-fixedpop.pdf}
\end{center}

Here clustering is strong enough that a plot can contain many trees or fall between clusters and contain none.

Compare the same four designs, including **four random plots west and five east**. For stratification, again add the two estimated half-region totals.

## Clustered populations increase uncertainty

\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.98\textwidth]{figures/juniper/cluster-histograms-fixedpop.pdf}
\end{center}

The population is held fixed while survey locations vary. The red line is the true abundance, $N=500$.

## Clustered populations increase uncertainty

Results from 2,000 repeated surveys:

```{r cluster-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(cluster_summary, digits = c(NA, 1, 0),
             col.names = c("Sampling design", "Mean estimate", "Variance"))
```

\vspace{0.3cm}

- clustering can produce highly variable counts under all four designs
- systematic plots spread effort; stratification samples both halves
- preferential placement is not representative and can be biased in either direction


# A probability model for count data$^*$

## How do we find the sampling distribution?

Clearly knowing the sampling distribution is an important aspect of determining the performance of an estimator. But, we cant repeat our survey many times. So how do we find it?

- need a probability model for the data generating process
- a model that encodes how we assume the data came about
- connects true abundance and the survey data
- can then deduce estimator performance
- can also use the probability model to construct estimators

## The binomial model for counts

A binomial model counts the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials.

**Example 1:** Flip a fair coin 3 times. What is the probability of getting 2 heads?

- $N=3$ trials; a head is a “success”
- Each flip has $p=0.5$ for heads and $1-p=0.5$ for tails

\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.1}
\begin{tabular}{ccc}
\textbf{Sequence} & \textbf{Multiply the flip probabilities} & \textbf{Probability} \\
HHH & $0.5 \times 0.5 \times 0.5$ & $0.125$ \\
\textcolor{red}{HHT} & \textcolor{red}{$0.5 \times 0.5 \times 0.5$} & \textcolor{red}{$0.125$} \\
\textcolor{red}{HTH} & \textcolor{red}{$0.5 \times 0.5 \times 0.5$} & \textcolor{red}{$0.125$} \\
HTT & $0.5 \times 0.5 \times 0.5$ & $0.125$ \\
\textcolor{red}{THH} & \textcolor{red}{$0.5 \times 0.5 \times 0.5$} & \textcolor{red}{$0.125$} \\
THT & $0.5 \times 0.5 \times 0.5$ & $0.125$ \\
TTH & $0.5 \times 0.5 \times 0.5$ & $0.125$ \\
TTT & $0.5 \times 0.5 \times 0.5$ & $0.125$ \\
\end{tabular}

\textcolor{red}{Exactly 2 heads: $0.125 + 0.125 + 0.125 = 0.375 = 37.5\%$}
\end{center}

## The binomial model for counts

**Example 2:** There are 3 animals in a population. A survey has a 20\% chance of detecting each animal (independently). What is the probability of detecting 2 animals?

- $N=3$ trials; D = detected (success), M = missed
- Each trial has $p=0.2$ for detected and $1-p=0.8$ for not detected

\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.1}
\begin{tabular}{ccc}
\textbf{Sequence} & \textbf{Multiply the detection probabilities} & \textbf{Probability} \\
DDD & $0.2 \times 0.2 \times 0.2$ & $0.008$ \\
\textcolor{red}{DDM} & \textcolor{red}{$0.2 \times 0.2 \times 0.8$} & \textcolor{red}{$0.032$} \\
\textcolor{red}{DMD} & \textcolor{red}{$0.2 \times 0.8 \times 0.2$} & \textcolor{red}{$0.032$} \\
DMM & $0.2 \times 0.8 \times 0.8$ & $0.128$ \\
\textcolor{red}{MDD} & \textcolor{red}{$0.8 \times 0.2 \times 0.2$} & \textcolor{red}{$0.032$} \\
MDM & $0.8 \times 0.2 \times 0.8$ & $0.128$ \\
MMD & $0.8 \times 0.8 \times 0.2$ & $0.128$ \\
MMM & $0.8 \times 0.8 \times 0.8$ & $0.512$ \\
\end{tabular}

\textcolor{red}{Exactly 2 animals: $0.032 + 0.032 + 0.032 = 0.096 = 9.6\%$}
\end{center}

## The binomial model for counts

The probability of getting $n$ successes out of $N$ trials, each with success probability $p_c$ is 
$$
\underbrace{f(n)}_{
  \substack{
    \text{Probability of } n \text{ successes}\\
    \text{from } N \text{ trials}
  }
}
=
\overbrace{\binom{N}{n}}^{
  \substack{
    \text{Number of different sequences}\\
    \text{of length } N \text{ with } n \text{ successes}
  }
}
\underbrace{p_c^n}_{
  \substack{
    \text{Probability of}\\
    n \text{ successes}
  }
}
\overbrace{(1-p_c)^{N-n}}^{
  \substack{
    \text{Probability of}\\
    N-n \text{ failures}
  }
}
$$

\vspace{1em}

- \alert{Easy to calculate $f(n)$ in R!}

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 10; N <- 20; p <- 0.3 
dbinom(n, N, p)
```

<!---
\let\thefootnote\relax\footnotetext{this is standard and can be looked up on, eg, \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_distribution}{wikipedia}}
--->

## The binomial model for counts

- Assumptions of the binomial model:
    - fixed number of trials $N$, 
    - trials are independent, 
    - each trial has the same success probability $p_c$ 

\vspace{2em}

- Properties of the binomial model:
    - expected value: $\mathbb{E}(n)=Np_c$
    - variance: $\text{Var}(n)=Np_c(1-p_c)$
    - from this we can work out that the estimator for $\hat{N}$ is unbiased
    - and calculate its variance

## Maximum likelihood estimators

Maximum likelihood estimators can be used for any model where you can write down the likelihood.

- $\theta$ is the parameter or parameters of interest
- $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$ is the likelihood function: 
    - it's a function of the parameter(s) $\theta$
    - it's the probability of observing data given a specific value of $\theta$
    - eg, *probability of observing 20 juniper trees if* $N=100$

## Binomial example using the juniper point transects

Reminder of the nine circular plots (point transects) and data:

- juniper trees observed: $n = 20$
- proportion of region covered: $p_c = 15.90/100 \approx 0.159$
- inference objective: estimate the true abundance $N$

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=-1.8cm] at (current page){
\includegraphics[height=1.8in]{figures/region-with-plots-with-samplesize}};
\end{tikzpicture}

## Binomial example using the juniper point transects

Reminder of the nine circular plots (point transects) and data:

- juniper trees observed: $n = 20$
- proportion of region covered: $p_c = 15.90/100 \approx 0.159$
- inference objective: estimate the true abundance $N$

\vspace{0.5cm}

Suppose a binomial model and use the likelihood function (binomial PMF) to calculate probability of observing 20 for any value of $N$

$${\mathcal{L}}(N)= \binom Nn p_c^n(1-p_c)^{(N-n)}$$

## Binomial example using the juniper point transects

Reminder of the nine circular plots (point transects) and data:

- juniper trees observed: $\hig{n = 20}$
- proportion of region covered: $p_c = 15.90/100 \approx \hir{0.159}$
- inference objective: estimate the true abundance $N$

\vspace{0.5cm}

Suppose a binomial model and use the likelihood function (binomial PMF) to calculate probability of observing 20 for any value of $N$

$${\mathcal{L}}(N)= \binom {N}{\hig{20}} (\hir{0.159})^{\hig{20}}(1-\hir{0.159})^{N-\hig{20}}$$

\let\thefootnote\relax\footnotetext{note: ${\mathcal{L}}(\theta)=0$ for $N<20$ because $n$ cannot be larger than $N$}

## Binomial example using the juniper point transects

Reminder of the nine circular plots (point transects) and data:

- juniper trees observed: $\hig{n = 20}$
- proportion of region covered: $p_c = 15.90/100 \approx \hir{0.159}$
- inference objective: estimate the true abundance $N$

\vspace{0.5cm}

Suppose a binomial model and use the likelihood function (binomial PMF) to calculate probability of observing 20 for any value of $N$

$${\mathcal{L}}(N)= \binom {N}{\hig{20}} (\hir{0.159})^{\hig{20}}(1-\hir{0.159})^{N-\hig{20}}$$

- $N$ is the only unknown
- can use this function to find the \alert{maximum likelihood estimate}

\let\thefootnote\relax\footnotetext{note: ${\mathcal{L}}(\theta)=0$ for $N<20$ because $n$ cannot be larger than $N$}

## How many juniper trees?

$${\mathcal{L}}(N)= \binom {N}{\hig{20}} (\hir{0.159})^{\hig{20}}(1-\hir{0.159})^{N-\hig{20}}$$

- evaluate the likelihood function at a range of potential values of $N$
- find the $N$ that gives the highest likelihood of $n=20$
- this is the maximum likelihood estimator
- easy to do in `R`

\vspace{0.5cm}

```{r, size="footnotesize"}
n <- 20
p <- 0.159

N <- seq(20,250)
Lik <- dbinom(n,N,p) # vectorised R function
```


## How many juniper trees?

$${\mathcal{L}}(N)= \binom {N}{20} (0.159)^{20}(1-0.159)^{N-20}$$

```{r juniper-likelihood, echo=FALSE, results='hide'}
N <- seq(20,250,1)
Lik <- numeric(length(N))
n <- 20
p <- 0.159
Lik <- dbinom(n,N,p) # vectorised R function
likdf <- data.frame(Likelihood = Lik,
                    Abundance = N)

likplot <- ggplot(likdf, aes(Abundance, Likelihood)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_segment(aes(xend=Abundance, y=0, yend=Likelihood), color="grey") +
  geom_point(size=3, color=rd, fill=alpha(rd, 0.3), shape=21,stroke=1) +
  labs(y = "Likelihood (L(N))", x = "Abundance (N)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.margin = unit(c(1,1,1,1), "cm"),
        axis.title.y = element_text(margin = unit(c(0, 3, 0, 0), "mm"))) +
  transition_reveal(Abundance)
# The static plot below is regenerated from the juniper data when rendering.

likplot_static <- ggplot(likdf, aes(Abundance, Likelihood)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend=Abundance, y=0, yend=Likelihood),color="grey") +
  geom_segment(aes(x=Abundance[which.max(Likelihood)],xend=Abundance[which.max(Likelihood)],
                   y=0, yend=max(Likelihood))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(aes(x=Abundance[which.max(Likelihood)],
                 y=max(Likelihood)),size=2, color=rd, fill=alpha(rd, 0.3), shape=21, stroke=1) +
  labs(y = "Likelihood (L(N))", x = "Abundance (N)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.margin = unit(c(1,1,1,1), "cm"),
        axis.title.y = element_text(margin = unit(c(0, 3, 0, 0), "mm")))

ggsave(plot = likplot_static, filename = "figures/juniper/likelihood.png", device = "png", width = 5.5, height = 4, units = "in", dpi=600)
```

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=-1.5cm] at (current page){
\includegraphics[width=0.6\textwidth]{figures/juniper/likelihood.png}};
\end{tikzpicture}

## How many juniper trees?

The maximum likelihood estimate is the value of $N$ that gives the maximum likelihood of our observation of 20 with $p_c=0.159$: $\hat{N} = 125$.

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=-1.55cm] at (current page){
\includegraphics[height=1.75in]{figures/juniper/likelihood.png}};
\end{tikzpicture}

How much uncertainty is there around this estimate?

# Confidence Intervals

## Beyond point estimates

We just discussed using maximum likelihood estimators to generate point estimates of parameters of interest, \alert{but we should never present point estimates without some measure of uncertainty}!

- having defined a probability model for the data generating process, we have everything we need to define the sampling distribution
- prefer not to work with the whole sampling distribution
- common practice is to present a \alert{confidence interval}

\begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay]
\node[xshift=0cm, yshift=-2.5cm] at (current page){
\includegraphics[height=1.0in]{figures/cheetah}};
\end{tikzpicture}

## Confidence intervals

The confidence interval is a very common way to quantify uncertainty

- \alert{estimates} of a lower and upper bound $(L,U)$
- both are a function of the data (*they are random variables*)

\vspace{0.5cm}

Basic idea is: for a parameter $\theta$, pick estimators $L$ and $U$ to satisfy:
$$\mathbb{P}(L<\theta<U) = \alpha$$

- True $\theta$ lies between $L$ and $U$ is $\alpha$ of the time
- for a 95% confidence interval, $\alpha=0.95$

## Remember the 'on average' interpretation

Imagine we could repeat surveys many times & record estimate each time

- generate a sampling distribution
- describes what we expect if we did the survey again
- \alert{same idea for confidence interval estimators}
    - $L$ and $U$ are also random variables
    - estimate the \alert{interval} each time
    - generate a \alert{distribution} of intervals

## Conceptual motivatation (via simulation)

Imagine we could repeat two surveys, each 100 times:

- assume a binomial data generating model
    - an unbiased estimator
    - variance shrinks with increasing sample size
    
- consider two surveys that differ in coverage (and hence variance)
    - survey 1: $N=250$ and $p_c=0.25$
    - survey 2: $N=250$ and $p_c=0.75$

- calculate the interval $(L,U)$ for each survey and replicate

```{r, echo=FALSE, results='hide', message=FALSE, error=FALSE}
set.seed(12345)
N <- 250
p <- c(0.25,0.75)
n <- matrix(NA,100,2)
lwr <- matrix(NA,100,2)
upr <- matrix(NA,100,2)

n[,1] <- rbinom(100,N,p[1])
lwr[,1] <- n[,1]/p[1] - 1.96*sqrt((n[,1]/p[1]) * ((1-p[1])/p[1]))
upr[,1] <- n[,1]/p[1] + 1.96*sqrt((n[,1]/p[1]) * ((1-p[1])/p[1]))
  
n[,2] <- rbinom(100,N,p[2])
lwr[,2] <- n[,2]/p[2] - 1.96*sqrt((n[,2]/p[2]) * ((1-p[2])/p[2]))
upr[,2] <- n[,2]/p[2] + 1.96*sqrt((n[,2]/p[2]) * ((1-p[2])/p[2]))

pdf(file="figures/intervals.pdf",width = 8, height = 5)
par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(4,1,1,1), oma=c(0,0,0,0))
plot(0,0,type="n", xlim=c(100,400), ylim=c(1,100), main="", 
     xlab="Abundance", axes=FALSE)
box(bty="o")
axis(1)
abline(v=250)
segments(x0=lwr[,1],y0 = 1:100, x1 = upr[,1],y1 = 1:100, 
         col=ifelse(upr[,1]<250 | lwr[,1]>250, rd,bl), 
         lwd=ifelse(upr[,1]<250 | lwr[,1]>250, 2, 1))

plot(0,0,type="n", xlim=c(100,400), ylim=c(1,100), main="", 
     xlab="Abundance", axes=FALSE)
box(bty="o")
axis(1)
abline(v=250)
segments(x0=lwr[,2],y0 = 1:100, x1 = upr[,2],y1 = 1:100, 
         col=ifelse(upr[,2]<250 | lwr[,2]>250, rd, bl), 
         lwd=ifelse(upr[,2]<250 | lwr[,2]>250, 2, 1))
dev.off()
```

## Confidence intervals

- a distribution of 100 95% confidence intervals (ie, $\alpha=0.95$)
    - these are random intervals
    - most include true value (\textcolor{bl}{---}), but some don't (\textcolor{rd}{---})
    - proportion holds across levels of variance

\end{tikzpicture}



## Confidence intervals

- in general $x\%$ of confidence intervals calculated at the $x\%$ confidence level will include the true parameter value. 
    - 95% of the 95% confidence intervals will include truth
    - 90% of the 90% confidence intervals will include truth
    - if assumptions are met

\end{tikzpicture}


## How to calculate the intervals?

For large samples, and under the usual regularity conditions, MLEs are approximately normally distributed:

$$\hat{N} \;\dot\sim\; \text{Normal}\bigl(N,\text{Var}(\hat{N})\bigr).$$

- The variance $\text{Var}(\hat{N})$ measures how much the estimate varies between repeated surveys.
- **Different sampling designs require different variance calculations**: simple random, stratified random, and systematic sampling.
